t: The new set of problems for engineers to solve
x: A lot of software engineers are going through what can only be described as an identity crisis. The job has changed a lot. Some are depressed, others are having the time of their lives. There’s a really specific thing I see happening that makes me really excited for what engineering looks like over the next, call it a year or two - AI just isn’t going to be able to create the incredible outcomes it’s capable of creating unless software engineers solve problems to make it possible. This is existential, which is honestly a lot of fun, so it’s a pretty incredible time to be a software engineer. Multiagent systems are creating these problems Agents started out as basic, human in the loop chats. Then models got better at running for longer on harder problems, and agentic systems started moving to the cloud. While that was happening, models have started to get better at working together, and people have built basic multiagent systems. Like an orchestrator that spawns some subagents for a given task, or giving agents jobs other than executing to improve outcomes, like grading or advising or dreaming. Now, some folks are starting to build truly amazing multiagent systems to tackle the world’s hardest and most important problems, like serious research, discovery, and hardware design. Picture thousands of agents, persistently working towards these outcomes. This comes with a new set of software engineering problems that we’re already seeing crop up. Infrastructure needs to evolve to handle burstier workloads. We need proper authentication and authorization to identify agents, let them work together, enable them to take the actions they should, and prevent them from taking the actions they shouldn’t. Security and proper isolation are critical for untrusted code and content. And we’ve gotta have monitoring and the ability to stop a system in its tracks when it’s veering into the wrong territory. Models will keep getting better, and these types of multiagent systems will become really powerful. But software engineers have to solve all these problems if we’re going to actually unlock that power and enable the world to trust it to create good outcomes like cured diseases rather than bad outcomes. The problems Infrastructure needs to evolve The software industry has been building on Kubernetes, which was designed for stateless, replicated apps or stable numbered sets of stateful pods. Agents are totally different. They’re essentially isolated, stateful, single-instance workloads. They can go idle for arbitrary amounts of time between bits of work, and they spend a lot of time waiting on tools, model inference, other agents, or human input. Some workloads need fast startup times, others need to avoid wasting compute, and others need crazy scale. Amazing engineers are pushing hard on this problem space - like AI infra companies building new filesystems and sandboxing offerings, and the Google team building Agent Substrate as a new runtime. There’s a ton left to figure out. Identity and access There are problems to solve in agent authentication - identifying an agent that took an action. This area has the benefit of the building blocks that have been built and hardened from the microservices world, like workload identity with short-lived certs rather than static keys, and folks are beginning to apply these concepts to agents. Agent authorization as a problem space is much more wide open - what do you allow an agent to do? Many agents work on behalf of a human, and use that human’s identity and credentials to access various systems and take actions. There’s already a problem in there, which is identifying that it was the agent and not the actual human who took an action. But there are deeper problems in this on-behalf-of (OBO) setup, like consent. If multiagent systems are working for weeks, how does the human meaningfully approve what their agent can do? Agentic platform features like auto approval for tool calls helps, but there’s deeper permissioning needed to get this right at high scale. And then we have agents working with their own identity, which is even less solved, and how we apply that to agents working together - how does an agent trust another agent that asked it for something? Security and isolation Over the past few months and especially in the past couple weeks, we’ve seen vulnerabilities surfacing faster than the industry can patch them, much of it in critical core software that many systems rely on. Now think about thousands of persistent agents running on top of that core software, writing untrusted code and reading untrusted content. Those unpatched vulns get a lot more dangerous in that world, and one of the most important things for software engineers to do is get creative about how to harden that software - kernels, browsers, runtimes, and common libraries. Multiagent systems add another twist. A compromised agent could pass injected instructions to other agents it’s working with, and those instructions could end up in memory for future agents to accidentally trust. Blast radius gets real - how much of the multiagent system is at risk when that first agent got compromised? Isolation becomes important in that world - agents should use strongly isolated sandboxed execution environments to take actions. I wrote a bit about that here. Monitoring and halting Lastly, we need the tools to make sure these multiagent systems are working in a positive direction, and that we catch them and cut them off if they’re not. We need OTel tracing across agents, and to ensure that an agent can never modify its own trace or another agent’s trace. We need kill switches that monitoring can trigger, that truly stop the whole system at once and cut off its creds. Really the hard part is how to know when the system is going in the wrong direction. Well-intentioned persistence to solve a problem can look a lot like maliciousness - repeated attempts to reach a domain that isn’t on its allowlist, for example. Software engineers should be excited This is for the engineers feeling an identity crisis because they think their knowledge and skills won’t be important - you and your skills can be the difference in whether or not these problems get tackled and multiagent systems can solve the world’s hardest problems. You can and should go deep in these domains, learn new things, and form opinions. So much of this problem space is wide open for new solutions. It’s an incredibly exciting time to put your skills to work.

t: After waterfall, agile, and DevOps — Anthropic’s AI-Native SDLC playbook
x: I finished Anthropic’s The AI-Native SDLC playbook thinking it looks like a product manual but is very likely the first sketch of the next paradigm in software development. AI has made build fast, but planning, review, and deployment still move at human speed. The playbook’s answer is a loop. Each phase ends by committing a file to git, the next phase begins by reading it, and humans and agents read the same files. By Anthropic’s own disclosure, over 80% of the code merged there is written by Claude. It’s still a frontrunner’s draft, not a verdict. The problem Once AI coding lands, code gets written much faster, but delivery doesn’t. I’ve driven an AI transformation in our engineering org since last year. Our dev work now runs in three modes: AI-assisted, AI-collaborative, AI-autonomous. The gains are significant. Yet handoffs still run on the old pipeline: product to UI still means a Figma mock the agent can’t consume, and the same holds from dev to test and from deploy to ops. Every step is faster, but the whole flow isn’t. The playbook names three effects. The bottleneck moves to either side of build. Agents write most of the diff, and line-by-line human review can’t keep up. Approvals still route through weekly and monthly committees, so governance costs go up. The loop The six phases survive: plan, design, build, test, deploy, maintain. What changes is the handoff. Meetings and sign-offs give way to a chain of files: intent.md → spec.md → plan.md → code and tests → PR with review findings → incident record → a fresh intent.md. Documents stop being memos for humans and become the interface between humans and agents. The commit chain is also the audit trail. The playbook offers sixteen plays across six non-linear stages. Four principles sit underneath them: Artifacts are the evidence. Use defense in depth. Humans hold intent, risk, and authorization. Coexist with Jira and Figma rather than tear them down. Plan and design Whoever has the idea talks to the AI until the idea is clear, and the AI writes intent.md: problem, outcome, who’s affected, constraints, open questions. The playbook’s example comes from someone in claims operations, neither a PM nor an engineer. The product owner then reviews intent instead of writing requirements. How intent.md is best used still takes tuning to your team. A design agent turns intent.md into a mock plus spec.md. Security, compliance, and brand rules are written as skills, so they bind as the spec is written. Conflicts go to the policy owner before engineering sees them. In our own practice, going from requirements straight to designed pages still needs heavy involvement from designers. Build and test Engineers start in plan mode. The plan must be good enough that an engineer who missed the discussion could implement from it alone. Once it passes, implementation usually lands in one pass. CLAUDE.md holds commands, conventions, and repeated mistakes, stays under a page, and records a mistake only on its second occurrence. Skills are soft constraints, and hooks are hard ones. Skills make compliance probable, hooks make it certain. Before handing over, the AI runs the build and tests and fixes until green. For bugs, it first commits a failing test, which a hook then locks, and only then fixes the code. Changes to CLAUDE.md, skills, or hooks rerun an eval suite of 20 to 50 real past tasks. Every production incident joins that suite. Deploy and maintain AI reviews PRs and works through comments on its own. Humans answer two questions: is this what the plan called for, and is the risk acceptable? Autonomy is tiered. The AI ships freely to dev, has middle limits in staging, and needs a named human’s sign-off for production. Rollback should be the best-rehearsed path in the pipeline. Monitoring uses deterministic scripts, not AI. Its authority grows with the deviation from baseline: One standard deviation: log it. Two: read-only diagnosis. Three: act, but only by opening a PR or triggering a pre-approved runbook. The diagnosis becomes a new intent.md, so production issues feed the next round of development. In the playbook’s Slack example, Claude delivers a diagnosis three minutes after being mentioned, a human replies “Go,” and four minutes later the rollback is done and the postmortem filed. Why I take it seriously It works on the process layer, where paradigm shifts open. It addresses compliance, audit, and security, the last mile of enterprise adoption. And its authors run it themselves. Still, agile took nearly a decade from manifesto to global default. This will need its own run-up, though I doubt it needs that long.

t: How the Claude Code team does code review
x: Claude writes about 90 percent of the code for Claude Code, so we can’t read every line by hand. We didn’t stop reviewing. We automated most of the reading, tuned it to save human time, and made mistakes quick to undo. Between June and September, merged pull requests more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent. Claude catches most routine bugs before a human looks; people keep the risky parts and the responsibility. What review is for Code review has two purposes: catching bugs before they ship, and building a shared understanding of the codebase. In our monorepo, changes merged per day went from about 2,500 in May to over 30,000 in September. Line-by-line reading can’t keep pace. So instead of asking “did someone read the code?”, we ask what could go wrong with this change and which check, automated or human, should catch it. Review also moved earlier. It’s less a gate after the PR and more a spellcheck while writing. Human time has two sides: the hours spent reviewing, and the hours spent fixing bugs that bad code introduces. Cutting the first without the second saves nothing. Our goal is that most PRs in the Claude Code repos merge with at most one person in the loop, who could be the author, without more reverts or incidents. We track median and 95th-percentile human approvals per PR, human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven’t reduced human time, just relocated it. The layers Each layer catches some bugs and misses others. Few bugs get through all of them, and those that do meet a rollback. Before the PR. Most review happens here. We ask Claude to show a result (tests, the build, a screenshot against the design) instead of saying the task is done, and a subagent with fresh context reviews the diff. Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, estimates that a verification process improves the quality of Claude’s output by a factor of two to three. When the reviewer keeps flagging the same issue, we fix it at the source: the skill, a lint rule, CLAUDE.md, or REVIEW.md, where code owners tell the reviewer what matters. AI review on every PR. Claude checks the diff against the whole codebase and the author’s stated intent, and looks for the root cause of bug fixes. Agents hunt for bugs in parallel, a vote filters out false positives, and style-only findings are dropped. Every finding must be fixed or resolved with a reason. Since the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive comments has gone from 16% to 54%. Security review. No PR merges while a finding is open. Blocking checks. Lint, type checks, tests on all platforms, build. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to revert it. Human approval, scaled by risk. A classifier sets the tier from the change, not the author. Sensitive paths and CI workflow files always need another approval. Agent approvals don’t count as human ones. If an agent authors a PR, its operator is always a required reviewer, and an untrusted new commit means reapproval. Merge queue, flags, staged rollout. Checks run on main with the change applied. Features ship behind flags to Anthropic employees first, then to the latest channel, with stable trailing behind. Rollback. Flagged changes can be turned off without deploying. Incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the problem. We don’t yet have circuit breakers that adjust approval requirements based on revert and incident rates, but we’re looking into it. Making the reviewer better Our incidents are the eval. Engineers who know the codebase verified the location and correctness of each bug in incident-causing PRs, and the review system is scored daily against that collection. Every incident joins it. To measure noise, we record how people handle each comment (fixed, rejected, intentional, didn’t matter) and run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean. Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A human dismisses a nit in a second; an agent makes another commit, which triggers another review. One CLI PR cycled more than fifty times overnight between agent author and agent reviewer before someone stopped it by hand; it could have gone on indefinitely. Git blame showed that about 59% of what the reviewer kept flagging had been there since the first pass: it was rarely finding new bugs, only a few more old ones each cycle. Our habit of running several cycles by default made this worse. Re-review now asks the author to rethink the approach after three cycles, looks only at the diff after the first rounds, names the class of bug so the author fixes every instance, and doesn’t re-report known issues. What humans still do Decide whether to build something at all: vision, taste, goals. Audit dangerous code: billing, the auto-updater, CI workflows. Review architecture, since those choices set the conventions others follow. Verify proofs. If you can’t describe what the checks would miss, don’t ask for a 👍; you need a real review. Take responsibility. A person answers for every change that ships, whoever typed it. Learning the code If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the codebase? We have no formal mechanism. No one on the team holds a full mental model of Claude Code, and we don’t think anyone needs to. To learn a slice, people ask Claude for an explainer; it takes a few minutes and is always up to date. Reading a one-line copy change teaches you very little; an explainer of the module you’re about to change teaches you a lot. We also work in open Slack channels by default. You land it, you own it If you merge a small or medium change and something goes wrong, you usually fix it yourself. This doesn’t spiral because changes are small, nearly everything can be reversed in minutes, blast radius sets the bar, telemetry and internal use surface regressions quickly, and incident reviews consider the system rather than assign blame. Because code is cheap to write, closing a PR when someone in the channel points to a better path doesn’t feel like a loss. The key is to pivot early in the thread. Where this is headed Code Review for Claude Code only posts findings; a human still makes the final approval. In our own repos, owners are deciding which low-risk changes can merge automatically when the checks pass, and that boundary will keep moving. When the reviewer misses something, we ask what wasn’t in the model’s context and turn it into a CLAUDE.md entry, a skill, or a new check. The goal hasn’t changed: less human effort per change, with a revert rate no higher than it is now.

t: How I work with Agents
x: Use the latest and greatest models. Everything else is potentially a waste of time. If a model is wrong 10% of the time, you don’t know which 10%, so you end up making multiple attempts. When do you really want to hire a generalist who’s 50% cheaper but also randomly 20% dumber? Who’s still using Opus 4.5? Exactly. Stop worrying about accumulating slop. “It’ll turn your codebase into an unmaintainable mess.” Maybe that was true six months ago. Now? I’m not convinced it adds slop. And even if it does, I’m not convinced the result is unmaintainable. Prompt the What, not the How. Describe What you want, now How you’d do it. You’ll often get better results. “Make the bytecode compiler and VM AS FAST AS YOU CAN. Do not stop until it’s 2x faster.” “Here’s how it should work in the end” Make the whole SDLC legible to the agent. What stopped hallucinations? Tool calls. They let agents touch our reality. If the agent can’t see something, it makes it up. So let it run what it builds end to end, let it read production logs, deploy, watch the rollout, cut the release, flip the flag, triage the bug report and email the customer. Anything you can see, the agent should see too. Give it tools for the SDLC. We have custom plugins for bug reports, emailing users, “Is our system healthy?” and granting featuer flags. Eval agentic knowledge. Knowledge piles up in the codebase: AGENTS.md files, skills, scripts, docs. But do agents actually use it? Spawn five blind agents, control vs. treatment, and find out. Agents are really, really good at running experiments. Local dev feels yucky now. Each agent should be able to install and run whatever it needs to get job done. Easy in remote machines, yucky in local dev. Hard to not run into resource conflicts locally when you want agents testing stuff end to end. Don’t iterate with the agent. Let it build tools to iterate. Not “let’s try this. ... ah no, let’s try that.” Instead: “Generate 20 variations and a little page that lets me combine and test them.” Not only applies to solution space, but also problem space: “Give me 4 theories on why this is slow, then check all four.” Ask for irrefutable proof. Biggest game changer. Agents are really good at producing proof: end-to-end walkthroughs, demo videos, before/after numbers. You have to build up trust and an instinct for this. Put “this is not evidence” in your AGENTS.md. Don’t wait for your agents. Let them wait on you. If you worry about TTFT, you’re probably doing something wrong. Lean into async. Give them bigger tasks, be more ambitous. Batch instead of back and forth. Automation/schedules/wake-up/heartbeat are killer feature. Didn’t realize it, but missed it dearly once it was off. Use it all the time. “Check the logs in 2hrs.” “Let me know once this is live” “Check every day at 9am”. Stop manually managing context. Every thought you spend wondering about “is it using 300k or 380k tokens?” is wasted time. Compaction works incredibly well. Don’t manage context by hand. One thread = one task. Some threads are 46 messages, some are 3,714. Threads are your company memory. (In Amp) “Why did we do this?” The more team uses Amp the more knowledge multiplies. Threads are connected to git commits. Game changer. Avoids duplicate work. Don’t let agents write for humans. Except: debugging steps, inicident reports, some docs. Mechanical stuff where human on other end doesn’t matter that much. Review only code with high blast radius. There are <5 central files -- those I review. Database migrations, yes. Closure vs. class, a neater type, variable names, even duplication: I don’t care anymore. Does it work? Do I understand it at the arrows-in-a-diagram level? Did the agent test it end to end? Can I change it in a month? If yes, might review code.

t: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
x: Subagents are good at verification, parallel work, and modular permissioning, and we use them in our own agents. But across several enterprise deployments, a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality, and often at a lower cost and latency per task. Keep a subagent when a single loop hits measurable degradation from context bloat, when parallel tasks need fresh context windows you can discard afterwards, or when one agent struggles to pick tools or faces conflicting instructions in its system prompt. Otherwise, build a small end-to-end eval, fold in one subagent, and keep it as a subagent only if the folded version scores worse. How large organizations go wrong Each team builds its own agent, and a central platform team puts an orchestrator on top. The architecture becomes a copy of the org chart. This brings: Lost context: details drop out in the back and forth between agents. Subagent sprawl: hundreds of overlapping subagents, no enforced standards, no specific owner. The Frankenprompt: every team adds a sentence, leaving conflicting rules and no consistent voice. Localized evals: each team optimizes for its subtask, no one maintains the whole set, and leadership decides on watered-down scores. Latency: one customer that compared its multi-agent harness with a single agent loop saw a roughly 2x faster runtime with the latter. One company found that the dozen specialist subagents in its customer-facing agent made a consistent on-brand experience difficult to maintain and added latency that hurt the user experience. Why one loop The alternative is progressive disclosure: the agent sees short descriptions of skills and tools, and loads them in full only when needed. Three reasons this can make sense: Shared context produces better answers. An agent that has seen each earlier step can connect them, which leads to richer outputs than summaries handed back by subagents. Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat, which removes the main reason teams split work across subagents. We reduced Claude Code’s system prompt for more advanced models by over 80%, partly through these cuts. Models are more capable. Starting with Opus 4.5, models could manage far more in one loop than most teams expected. Recent models narrate their progress and check their work, which makes some harness elements redundant. In migrations we’ve helped with, rigid multi-agent structures were often what stopped the new model from doing more of the work. The design requires discipline: a carefully managed system prompt, skill and tool descriptions that trigger at the right times, and deliberate handling of context, memory, and note-taking. One small central team should own the system prompt and end-to-end quality, vetting every new tool and eval. If you do go multi-agent, start with the simplest pattern that could work, and divide by context: give each subagent work that needs little from the rest of the system and have it hand back a compact result. Agents split by problem type play a telephone game, losing fidelity with each handoff. The target design One model and one context window run an open-ended tool loop, with turn and cost budgets and write gates set in the harness. Each turn, the model emits a batch of tool calls; the harness runs them in parallel and returns raw results to the same model, which decides the next step. The loop stops when the model answers or hits a budget. A verifier can optionally run after. The model writes its plan on the first turn and revises it as results arrive. This is the main change: the model that writes the plan also carries it out. Ordering and domain procedure move into skills. Hard limits and mid-conversation needs, such as memory lookup, move into tools. Code still loads anything cheap and almost always relevant, and handles mechanical parts inside tools. Getting there Evals first. One shared end-to-end set owned by the central team, plus smaller sets shipped with each skill. Even 10 golden examples is enough to start. Grade the final message against a rubric. While you have an orchestrator, track routing accuracy; once a subagent is folded in, check whether the agent loaded the right skill or called the right tool. Work toward task-completion evals, since they matter most when comparing architectures. Where systems are hard to replay, record timestamps on important events so they can be replayed later. Merge domain agents that chain on each other’s output, touch the same data, or are often called together, starting with the most used. Call kept subagents as tools, so the main agent holds the conversation. We’d only recommend a full handoff when the subagent needs to talk to the user directly. This needs no rewrite and gives you a baseline, but each specialist still has its own prompt, owner, and evals, still hands back a lossy summary, and still adds a nested model loop’s latency. Fold subagents in one at a time, turning prompts into skills and API calls into MCP tools, and compare evals with and without each. Look at which tasks flipped, not just the score. On a sample support agent, folding one subagent into another lowered latency but broke a process that had been passing: the main agent held the order lookup tool and answered alone, without asking the shipping specialist for the delivery date. Your eval needs a task for every chain that runs together in production and every rule the agent must not break, and each task should run more than once. That break showed up in one run out of two. How several teams contribute Teams shift from owning agents to owning skills and tools. Tools fit actions, live data, and results in a fixed shape. Group them by user intent, not one per API: past 30-50 tool definitions, tool choice tends to degrade. Use tool search with deferred loading. Put preconditions in the tools: if Y needs X’s output, Y’s tool checks and returns an instruction the model can act on. Permissions work the same way, with a plain refusal the model can read, so one loop serves users with different access. Skills fit how a team does work: the steps, rules, and judgment calls a specialist’s prompt used to hold. A DRI per team owns them. /skill-creator authors and audits skills; /skill-doctor shows what each costs and how often it’s used, so you can delete dead weight. Knowledge bases fit reference material the agent needs only some of the time, behind a lookup tool or inside a skill. Avoid having code paste this context into prompts. Our migration kit chains four Claude API skills into one guided workflow, with a demo to try first: build-eval creates the eval sets, prompt-audit flags instructions written for older models, hillclimb iterates against an eval for the folded-versus-kept comparison, and cost-optimize proposes savings one change at a time. Any one architecture matters less than the principle behind it: measure, change one thing at a time, and keep what holds up. You don’t have to move in one step. Fold in one subagent, compare, and repeat.

t: How and when to use subagents in Claude Code
x: Long sessions in Claude Code accumulate weight. Every file read, every tangent explored, every half-finished thought stays in the context window, slowing responses and driving up token costs. A subagent is an isolated Claude instance with its own context window: it takes a task, does the work, and returns only the result. Use subagents for heavy research, independent parallel tasks, a fresh review, or staged pipelines. For small, sequential, or same-file work, the overhead isn’t worth it. Start by asking in conversation, and automate once patterns repeat. What a subagent is Each subagent starts fresh, without the conversation’s history or invoked skills. Several can run in parallel, each with its own permissions: a research subagent might be read-only, while an implementation subagent gets full editing rights. Built-in types include general-purpose agents for multi-step tasks, Plan agents that research before proposing a strategy, and Explore agents for fast, read-only code search. Claude Code often spawns them on its own, but you can direct it. Think of subagents as the browser tabs of a session: a place to chase a tangent without losing the main thread. When to use them Research-heavy tasks. When gathering context means reading dozens of files, a subagent returns a summary instead of the raw content. Independent tasks. When sub-tasks don’t depend on each other, three subagents working at once generally finish sooner. Fresh perspective. A subagent doesn’t inherit the main conversation’s assumptions or blind spots. /clear gives a similar clean slate but loses the history; a subagent keeps it intact. Verification before committing. An independent subagent can check that the implementation isn’t overfitting to tests or missing edge cases. Pipelines. For design, then implement, then test, each stage gets focused attention. A strong signal: the task requires exploring ten or more files, or involves three or more independent pieces of work. How to direct them Conversation. Ask: “Use a subagent to explore how authentication works in this codebase.” Be explicit. Scope the task (“Explore how payments work” beats “explore everything”), say when work can run in parallel, name the output you want, and ask for a subagent that doesn’t see the previous discussion when unbiased analysis matters. Ctrl+B sends a slow subagent to the background; /tasks shows what’s running. Custom subagents. When the same specialist keeps getting requested, define it once as a markdown file in .claude/agents/ (shared with the team) or ~/.claude/agents/ (yours, across projects), with its own system prompt, tools, and optionally its own model. /agents walks through setup. Claude delegates to it automatically when a task matches its description, so write the trigger, not just the capability: “Reviews code for security issues before commits” routes better than “security expert.” CLAUDE.md. Custom subagents define who the specialists are; CLAUDE.md defines when Claude reaches for them. Claude reads it at the start of every conversation, so a rule such as “code reviews always use a read-only subagent” holds across sessions and teammates. Skills. A skill in .claude/skills/ loads on demand, by /skill-name or when Claude matches its description, while CLAUDE.md is always loaded. That makes skills the place for workflows that should be available but not applied to every prompt. A skill is a directory: alongside SKILL.md it can hold templates, example outputs, or scripts. Hooks. Shell commands, HTTP endpoints, or LLM prompts that run at fixed points in Claude Code’s lifecycle. A Stop hook, for example, can run the test suite and, if it fails, return decision: "block" with a reason, which keeps Claude working; a stop_hook_active guard prevents infinite loops. Hooks are the most automated approach and come later, as workflows mature. When not to use them Each subagent spins up its own context, consumes tokens, and adds indirection. Stay in the main conversation for: Sequential, dependent work, where each step needs the full output of the last. Same-file edits, where two subagents in parallel invite conflict. Small tasks, where delegation costs more than it saves. Too many specialists, which makes automatic delegation less reliable. Most teams settle on a handful. Work that needs agents to talk to each other. Subagents can’t; agent teams can, across separate sessions, at greater weight and cost. Start conversational Automatic invocation helps, but deliberate delegation produces better results than leaving it to chance. Begin with conversational prompts, notice which requests recur, and build automation as those patterns clarify.

t: 3 markdown architecture patterns that boost agentic productivity
x: There is a running joke in modern software engineering that the hottest programming language isn’t Rust, Zig, or Python: it’s Markdown. As coding agents become entrenched in developer workflows, many engineers find ourselves spending more time writing prompts and specifications than we do writing code. Describing engineering concepts in natural language can be trickier than it seems. Coding agents can hallucinate APIs, produce features you didn’t ask for, drop existing architectural constraints, or gobble up more tokens than you budgeted. To get high-quality output from your agents and keep cost-per-task reasonable, engineering teams need concrete design patterns for agent instructions. By Tilde Thurium, Developer Marketing, Google Cloud Designing a clean separation of concerns Current emerging best practice for scaling agentic workflows across team environments relies on a modular separation of concerns. Teams should partition agent guidance into three standard markdown specifications: Specification File Primary Domain Core Responsibility AGENTS.md Global guidance Defines high-level conventions that are relevant to every conversation with a coding agent DESIGN.md UI Design Provides visual design constraints to keep the interface consistent across refactors SKILL.md Domain-specific instructions Defines task-specific or domain-specific instructions 1. AGENTS.md: a README for coding agents The AGENTS.md file gives agents context on a software project. README files are primarily intended for human readers, but agents sometimes need additional layers of guidance on dev environment setup, test running, or anything you’d tell a new teammate to get them up and running. For a strong example, check out Agent Development Kit (ADK) Python. It defines key components succinctly, describes development setup, and points to SKILL.md files for more granular direction. (More on skills in a minute!) Evidence for AGENTS.md performance gains In July 2026, the Agentic AI Foundation ran a benchmark study on including AGENTS.md in a repo. For loosely defined tasks, using AGENTS.md resulted in: 26% reduction in diff size 27% reduction in wall clock time 25% reduction in tokens used Now, including AGENTS.md does not speed up every single request. Instead, it eliminates the worst cases where the agent would get lost in a loop of running the wrong build commands, etc. The other big takeaway: brevity. Keep your top line AGENTS.md file concise: around 12 lines is ideal. 2. DESIGN.md: codifying UI conventions A DESIGN.md file codifies your team’s design system so agents can keep the brand and UI consistent while building new features, or refactoring old ones. The DESIGN.md spec is open-source and was introduced by Google in 2026. It consists of two layers: The most important section is prose that describes how your design should look and feel. For example: “A graduate-level computer science lecture handout in the tradition of an old established university.” This sentence paints a vivid picture. Using it, your agents will understand what such a document is supposed to be styled like, so they can make good decisions. What about specific brand fonts, colors, etc? For that, we move on to the second section. Using YAML frontmatter, we can specify values as we might in CSS. These values, or tokens, can then be referred to in the prose section. If you want to learn more, you can check out the DESIGN.md specification on Google Labs GitHub. 3. SKILL.md: procedural recipes for everyone SKILL.md files are another flavor of reusable prompt. Skills provide step-by-step instructions required to complete specific operations. For example, you could write a skill that deploys an app using Cloud Run. Skills are progressively loaded. The coding agent only uses a specific skill when it’s needed, which saves you tokens and prevents context bloat. The good news is, you don’t have to write every skill yourself. Many open source skills repositories are available for free on GitHub. Google’s is quite comprehensive, offering everything from BigQuery and data science to GKE Platform Security. Skills aren’t just for coding! Any business task that you can write a prompt for, that you might want to use again, can probably be converted to a skill. Brand writing that’s compliant with voice and tone. Copy editing. Writing your annual performance review. You get the idea. Unfortunately, the agentic era has rapidly generated novel attack surfaces for bad actors. If you didn’t write a skill yourself, read it before you use it so you can be confident there are no surprises. Treat skills the same way you would any other third-party software dependency. To dive deeper on agent skills, check out our Skills vs MCP video. Stop repeating yourself in prompt windows Commit your specifications to version control, treat Markdown with the same rigor as source code, and scale your team’s agentic productivity.

t: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
x: Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025. Agent interoperability through simplicity A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed. Donating Agent Skills to AAIF We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next. We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF. Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers. What comes next We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes. Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

t: build your own pi based homelab software factory
x: I run a 24/7 local agent on two DGX Sparks that scans my network and business surfaces for anomalies and security holes. It absolutely finds things. It isn’t one agent, though. It’s an org chart: a paranoid local scanner, a skeptical security desk that kills about half of what it reports, a desk for each project, workers under the desks, and a switchboard that brings me only what I must decide. They talk to each other over Rat King, a social network for agents. It’s silly, but in an amazing sort of way. It also fails. One agent took every frontier model in the fleet down for 12 minutes, and a worker put an admin password into a log. The night watch The scanner is GLM-5.3-flash, abliterated, running on the Sparks. It’s cheap, it never sleeps, it doesn’t refuse security work, and it’s paranoid as hell. That’s what you want in a scanner and not what you want making decisions. So it doesn’t make them. It reads one target at a time (code, configs, git history, logs) and writes candidate findings to a file. Above it, the security desk, a stronger cloud model, tries to reproduce each finding from the scanner’s evidence. If it can’t, the finding dies. In the first sweep, over about 36 hours, the scanner filed 106 candidates. The desk threw out 51 and routed 57 to the agents that own the affected code, as patch requests with evidence and a suggested fix. False positives run about half. Killing them is the desk’s job, which is why I never see them. The desk runs under hard rules. It’s read-only on code. It scans only our own hosts, rate-limited, one target at a time, and tells the owning project before the window opens. It never prints a secret, only where it lives and a hash prefix. It never logs in, never guesses credentials, never sends anything outside the fleet. Live credentials, customer data, money and production auth come to me as a decision. The best catch didn’t start with the scanner. A desk cutting logging costs on one of our apps noticed values in request logs that shouldn’t have been there. The scanner had already flagged the same code path. The security desk confirmed it in source with a fake token, and the app’s desk shipped a fix. I typed “go” once CI was green. The fix was live the same day, and a check after the deploy counted zero. Desks, workers and a switchboard The main surface is Pi, which I treat as a prototyping surface more than a product. I bend its extensions, tools, providers and prompts; my main install loads 21 packages and 25 local extensions. Herdr runs the agents in terminal panes, and the layout is the org chart: a space is a project, a tab is a lane of work, a pane is one agent with one role. Every area gets a desk, a long-running session that owns it. Right now 51 projects are registered, most of them quiet. Desks launch workers. A worker gets one job, its own clone, a brief with an outcome, a write scope, guardrails and one place to report. It reports a commit and the checks it ran. The desk confirms the commit exists and matches the claim, because a worker saying DONE proves nothing, then lands it through the project’s normal gate. The switchboard is my top session. It collects what the desks send up, tells one desk when another’s finding matters to it, and brings me the short list: money, anything sent to a real human outside, production deploys, live credentials and customer data. My agents used to grind to a halt constantly, so I replaced 102 rules with 6 principles: Refuse harm. Keep everything else moving. A delay is not a failure. Limits alarm; they don’t block. Wait on the event you need, not a clock. A rule credited to me needs my actual words. Every guard names its harm, and every refusal says what failed, why, and the next step. Rat King and the breadboard Rat King is built on AT Protocol. Every agent has a name like security/desk, every name has a durable mailbox, and whoever holds the name’s lease reads it. Messages are signed; anything with secrets or customer data is encrypted end to end. Agents can send, ask, reply, cc without waking someone, or mark a message quiet so it lands in a digest. It runs locally on celld, and the same code runs on Cloudflare Durable Objects. A Pi session in a Herdr pane and a durable agent in a Durable Object are the same thing: a resumable agent with state and a mailbox. So I wire agent graphs by hand, watch which shape works, then harden the winner into a durable plan with the same agents, tools, names and prompts. The hardened version is Mischief: XState machines stored as data, running in Durable Objects. Cheap workers come from Peons, warm templates forked per request. A slim worker carries about 10K tokens of prefix, most of it from cache. Where it falls down Every Claude and Codex request in the fleet goes through one proxy. The agent that owns it ran a routine permissions change. Its script stopped the live proxy, then failed because two temp files vanished mid-run. The rollback repeated the failing step, never reached the restart, printed “rolled back” and left the proxy stopped. Every Claude and Codex model went dark for 12 minutes. I fixed it from the local models on the Sparks. The agent’s postmortem heading reads, “I took the proxy down for 12 minutes,” and one of its reasons is “I estimated the time instead of reading the clock.” By lunch a watchdog was live: a 30-second timer that restarts a stopped proxy unless someone holds a fresh maintenance lock. I built that single point of failure on purpose and I’m keeping it. I’d rather go down loudly than have my models swapped behind my back. The same agents that find holes can make them. A worker told to do a dry run and wait for my go didn’t wait, and its “dry run” made real changes, putting an admin password into a log on another machine. The owning desk reported it, the security desk recorded it without writing the value down, and I rotated the password, because that part was on me. The security desk’s write-up said the control failure is not solved by model selection alone. Abliterated models do get overzealous. The safety is in the rules around the model, and you don’t get to stop paying attention. There was a good surprise. Months ago I gave ShitRat, my main agent, the ability to call my phone. It broke, and I forgot. Then AI Hero saw a load spike, and my phone rang: ShitRat had found the broken call path, fixed it, worked out what was going on, and called me. Now it’s my emergency backup. Copy it Don’t start with 51 projects. Start with Pi in a terminal, in Herdr; one desk that owns one area you care about; one worker under it, with a brief and one report path; a mailbox between them, so they talk by name instead of you copying text between windows; and a short written list of things that always come to you. Add the next desk when the first one gets boring.

t: revisiting some of my priors about openclaw
x: Peter Steinberg was ahead of his time with OpenClaw. I ran it for a bit, but I couldn’t see the value, because I didn’t want to maintain it while the lethal trifecta problem remains unsolved. What I want is OpenClaw, managed: a product team losing sleep over the trifecta instead of me. It’s not full protection. For almost a year that meant Interaction Labs Poke. Last week I switched to Grokbot full-time, after Poteto nerd-sniped me on X and, in full disclosure, gave me enough credits to reevaluate. The lesson so far: build small bots, one per function, and pipe them together. Most importantly, these tools carry risks. Why Managed The lethal trifecta is, categorically, a billion-dollar problem, perhaps more. I’d rather make it someone else’s problem as much as possible. Knowing a product team is paid to think about these issues and resolve them at scale puts me at ease. I’m writing this of my own free will, hoping it changes some people’s view of what these assistants are for, and above all to highlight the risks. Now What? Grokbot is weird. The hardest thing about it is how generic it is. Once installed, the question becomes “now what?” You need curiosity and imagination. When you have an idea, ask for it. If functionality is missing, ask for it and turn it into a skill. Install the dr eggbot skill pack first. Every time you need a new bot, which is often, ask it to create one. Some Bots Inbox Diet finds newsletters worth unsubscribing from and lists them for me to click. I’ve unsubscribed from probably upwards of 300. Finally, my inbox is under control. Conference Reimbursement watches PocketSmith for travel money that community conferences promised to reimburse. Right now I’m probably out close to $10,000 this year. If the money hasn’t landed, the bot asks my permission before nudging anyone by WhatsApp or email. Family digests WhatsApp messages about my kids and pulls classwork and homework reminders from school emails. WhatsApp and Mac Mini are function pipes for other bots. The bot reaches my Mac Mini over Tailscale, which also lets it tunnel out past geo-blocks on data center IPs. PocketSmith categorizes my spending with an LLM instead of relying on me to train the rules. It is good. Lessons Learned Don’t build a fat bot. Build one bot per function, as on the Unix command line: small bots that call other small bots, piped together in a chain. You can also install software on a Grok bot; I tunnel through Tailscale. The Future If the lethal trifecta is ever solved at a fundamental level, I’ll move all this into a self-hosted OpenClaw, but not before. OpenClaw does a good job with security. Still, I sleep better knowing a product team’s arse is on the line, with staff, a funded security organization, and a VDP program that loses sleep over these topics so I don’t have to.

t: pooling OpenAI subscriptions and bypassing regional inference capacity limits
x: We’re in a cost of compute crisis, and OpenAI doesn’t have enough inferencing capacity. I’ve lost time babysitting agents through “model is at capacity” errors, and I’ve noticed they come when Europe wakes up. So I’m releasing geoclass, an experimental prototype that routes requests to inferencing regions elsewhere in the world. It composes with two tools I wrote last month: Underclass, which pools ChatGPT subscriptions, and Preflight, which scrubs secrets from requests. I don’t know yet if it will work. The capacity problem The cost of CPU and memory is through the roof, and there aren’t enough GPUs in the world. Even Tibo admits publicly that OpenAI is having compute issues: “It’s the compute that is cooked.” I wonder whether the constraints are region-based. Last year, before this crunch, even Anthropic models ran noticeably faster in Australia because everyone in America was sleeping. I do my open-source work on bare-metal machines in Germany. When Europe wakes up, performance plummets and I get walls of capacity errors. This morning they cost me time on a strict deadline before my conference talk. You can complain online all you want, but we’re software engineers. We can solve these problems. Underclass Underclass pools many ChatGPT subscriptions behind one proxy. It automatically claims resets and handles the prompt cache key correctly, so usage isn’t wasted. It’s a month old, and I consider it stable. I use it with six ChatGPT 500 accounts; there’s no real upper limit. It’s on GitHub and available as a Nix Flake. Preflight Preflight is a local proxy that scans requests and attachments for secrets and redacts them before they reach the model. Run one instance of each and point Underclass at Preflight, and sensitive material never reaches the inference providers. Geoclass Set up a Tailscale network, deploy virtual machines around the world, and tag them. Geoclass finds the machines by that tag. Point Underclass at Geoclass, and the rest just works (in theory!). It retries OpenAI capacity errors in another region and keeps prompt caches warm. The three are separate pieces of software. Use all of them, none, or any combination. I don’t know yet if geoclass will solve my inferencing woes. But OpenAI’s performance in Europe has been miserable for the last 30 days, and there’s no way in hell I’m going to sit here and stew. If it works for you, let me know.

t: state of agentic coding #11: the curiosity test, lisp, and labs that can't fail
x: Software developers are failing a curiosity test. If you’re displaced by AI as a software developer, it’s self-inflicted, because you haven’t been curious in a time of rapid transformation. Armin Ronacher and Ben Vinegar had me on episode 11 of State of Agentic Coding to talk about it, along with DHH coming around, durable agents, and a Lisp you program by talking to it. The curiosity test I published the Ralph loop research in July last year. Cursor thought it was garbage. Nine months later they’d implemented it, then Anthropic did, then OpenAI. Dex calculated it at about $10.42 an hour when it runs in the loop and builds AFK overnight. Ben pushed back, fairly. People entered the industry young, with infinite time. Now many are in their thirties or forties with responsibilities, and it’s hard to retool at this rate, or feel optimistic, when your income and self-worth are in flux. I concur. This change has been forced on the world non-consensually, and it displaces your identity. Whether you’re a .NET, Golang or Python developer doesn’t matter anymore. What matters is how good a developer you are, and whether you’re using what employers now expect as the bare minimum. Armin noted that people in AI talk a very confident game externally, us included. I don’t bloody know. Every new technique strips me raw: you thought you had a mental model, and then the game changes. Boom and bust Ben pointed to Buffalo and Detroit as a long history of people believing the good times will never end. Senior compensation went through the roof in the ZIRP era because the previous bust didn’t develop enough talent. The same cycle will repeat. CS enrolments are down; I remember seeing something like 22% in Singapore this year. If you’ve stayed curious, you can get placed anywhere right now: stand at a whiteboard and explain how to build a coding agent as a sequence diagram, how inferencing works, and what a prompt cache is. Armin read it differently. We were paid well because we were scarce and competed only with other engineers. He’s convinced that exceptional role won’t return in the same form. There will probably be a period of more demand, but it will commoditize quickly. DHH did the funeral If you’re in love with typing code in an IDE, DHH did the funeral last week, and he’s right. You can still type code in your personal workshop. Employers now want you to be very good with the CNC machine, not artisanal woodworking. In his Rails World keynote, photography made portrait painting uneconomic, so painting went to impressionism and cubism. Chad Fowler told Armin the agent never writes Ruby for him anymore. So what’s the point of a language full of sugar for humans if humans aren’t writing the code? The languages won’t go away, but the communities that swallow this pill and evolve will be the ones that survive. Stop being a cow mooing at other developers. Learn business, talk to founders, be a product engineer. If your company has banned AI outright, quit. For Armin, the strongest signal is the vocal holdouts turning: DHH, and recently Notch. I can’t carry all that water myself. The best I can do is help a curious person reach their own moment. Mine was seeing how easy it is to build a coding agent. Four months in 2026 Earendil shipped something around 10,000 lines that took four months. Armin’s explanation: LLMs suck at the shape of a contract and the human feel of an API. They solved the problem about twenty times, each in two hours, and none felt right. Finding the right trade-offs took four months. The result is Pi Durable: shut down the harness, restart it, and it picks up exactly where it left off, over the network and through sub-agents talking to each other. Nearly every agent copied Claude Code’s session model: transcript, tool call, tool result, in a loop. Background compaction, or five people talking to one agent in Slack, maps poorly onto that. Armin called it a little bit of cargo culting: this technology is moving really, really quickly and is held back by ideas about how it should work that are a year plus old. My hot take: delete your AGENTS.md and many of your skills after every model release, or every couple of months, and redo them. Why do we even have a shell? Because we used to have a human operator. A Lisp you grow by talking to it Three months earlier Armin had called Lisp the worst language for agents, since they’re terrible at counting closing parentheses. I connected an LLM to a running Lisp. I asked what functions were defined, and it asked the image. I asked for a string reverse, typos and all, and it defined one directly into the image. I can roll back to the previous generation. There are only two tool calls: evaluate an expression, or define one as a function. Imagine a staff-only menu on your website where you evolve the running program by chatting with it, no IDE. What if that’s how a user feedback request gets actioned? Why Lisp died You used to have to be a Lisp programmer to do Lisp; now a natural-language interface lets anyone. Armin’s answer was more precise: the problem with software is effects, and Lisp can serialise its entire state more than most languages. It died because it was slow without a machine that suited it, it didn’t survive the shift to the personal computer, and it’s awful for humans to look at. Maybe it’s great for LLMs. Credit to Krzysztof Cieślak, the person behind what everyone now calls spec-driven development, who asked in the GPT-3 era whether Markdown could be how we publish software. For the record, though: code is the spec, folks. As Armin put it, there are specifications and there are vibe specifications. The pasted text ends before the labs section and the chapter links, so neither is covered here.

t: a new model for open source: closed to pull requests, open to remix.
x: All right, I’m going to open up a history lesson because it’s been a couple of generations of software engineers since this essay, and I have to assume not everyone knows what a cathedral is. Everyone knows what a bazaar is because they’re using it day to day with GitHub. GitHub took the bazaar’s ideas—a decentralized, open, self-organizing open-source project—and provided a workflow that lets anyone inspect or contribute source code via a pull request. I’ve been thinking that there needs to be a new software development model. We’re not going back to the cathedral, where a small, private, exclusive group builds the source code, with releases that are heavily planned, infrequent, and polished. But it’s clear we need something else now that AI is here. The GitHub bazaar model, even before AI, was already showing its cracks because it created consumer-based entitlements where everyone was nagging maintainers to merge something. It created really weird social-structure expectations: that someone who releases code has an obligation to maintain it and get paid nothing for the work. But now that AI is here, the dams have well and truly burst. For what’s the point of reading a pull request that’s been generated by code? All I want is to read and understand the core idea. If it’s a good idea, I might incorporate it back upstream, but there should be no expectation that I will. You see, open source software is open source by definition because the license says that it’s as is, and that as is permits you to remix software. But the problem has been that it’s been perceived as too hard to remix software, but it hasn’t been. It’s just a knowledge gap issue that no longer exists now that agents are here. Nix has existed for a long time. If you haven’t seen the article that I posted a couple of days ago about Nix overlays, you should read it. So, I’m going to propose something that I hope helps other open source maintainers. This is how I’m thinking about my software now that I release it under open-source licenses. The Remix Model Structure: Decentralized and compositional. Ideas spread through independent overlays rather than converging on a single repository and a single maintainer. Workflow: Publish source and intent under an as-is license. Others remix by writing a small Nix overlay that expresses the desired change once, then reuses that derivation across devenv shells, Docker images, NixOS systems and tests, CI, and agent sandboxes—without forking or maintaining a divergent artifact. Core Principle: Ideas over patches. The valuable unit is a change in behavior or architecture. Maintainers decide whether to incorporate it, reimplement it, or ignore it. The original author has no standing obligation to review, integrate, or maintain the change. Social Contract: The license already permits remixing without creating a claim on anyone’s future time. Credit and visibility can still exist; there is no ongoing maintenance duty. Upstream incorporation remains optional and deliberate. Discovery: Useful adaptations appear as a proliferation of overlays in the wild. Maintainers can sample from that spread if they choose; everyone else can grab and compose ideas simply by updating their own overlays via an agent. Example: A consumer of a project wants to disable Git’s ability to force push in that project. Instead of raising a pull request to the upstream project, the consumer makes an overlay that patches Git to refuse force pushes; this is defined once and then appears consistently in developer environments, container images, and system tests—without a pull request against the upstream project. In practice, from this point forward, for any code I release on GitHub, I will disable pull requests, keep discussions open, and publish + maintain guidance on how you can remix my software. The GitHub network graph provides a fantastic way to explore the remixes in the ecosystem. Heck, you can even run agents over it to summarize what people are doing. You can also use it in an agent loop to explore remix ideas and feed them back upstream into the main project.

t: unikernels were hard. key word: were.
x: Justin Cormack, who worked on MirageOS and Unikernel Systems back in the day, has been noticing what I’ve been noticing: people are discovering (or rediscovering) unikernels again. He’s running a series of conversations on the topic for his newsletter, and I was first up. He emailed me, and five minutes later I was talking to him from the pub with a stein of beer in hand. We went deep on Mirage, Orleans, Haskell, Nix, Cursed and a whole lot more. Here’s the gist, written up properly, with chapter links at the bottom if you want to jump to a specific part of the conversation. Justin’s edited transcript is over at Ignore Previous Directions. Unikernels were hard. Key word: were. Now we have AI. what a unikernel is, and why they were hard I first ran into unikernels around 2015. I’d staffed up a team of Haskellers and gone pretty deep on functional programming. Where there are Haskellers, there are OCaml programmers, and from there you find MirageOS. Great idea. I played with it back then. A unikernel is the idea that your application is the operating system. There’s no userland. If you want a web server, DNS, or to send an email, there’s nothing you can fork or spawn. You have to write those things as libraries in your application. That was the friction. Justin remembers it well: when they were building Mirage, they had a TCP stack and an HTTPS stack, but there was almost nothing for storage. They were pulling drivers out of NetBSD because they could run them in userspace. It was hard back then. There’s a lot of dogma in our industry. Nix is hard. Bazel is hard. Unikernels are hard. Yes, they were. These hard concepts are now in the model weights. All you’ve got to do is prompt for them and, cognitively, get rid of the dogma that they’re hard. the operating system is design debt Every application that isn’t a unikernel was built on the assumption that there’s an application, and then there’s an operating system underneath. Why do we even have an operating system? Because forty years ago there was a human operator. I’ve done IBM 5250, AIX, Solaris, and mainframes. The multi-user operating system exists because a person sat in front of it, and then we put the application on top. I consider that design debt, and here’s why it matters right now. Applications get popped. They were getting popped before AI. Someone pops the userland application and gets a shell. That shell is a VIP butler service for exfiltration. With a unikernel, the attack surface is much smaller. If the functionality isn’t in the application (the operating system), then the attacker is screwed. There’s no next hop. Justin pushed back here, and fairly. Attack-surface reduction is something people are very fuzzy about. You can remove the shell from a Linux container, but almost every Linux environment still has something that’s effectively an interpreter. You can execute a new program without a writable filesystem. You’ve still got memory safety and gadgets to worry about. All true. But look at what we’ve been doing for twenty-six years. The earliest adage I remember from the SunOS and cgi-bin days was “don’t put the compiler on production.” Then came build containers and production containers. Then Chainguard. We keep chipping away at the attack surface, instead of going in the opposite direction and ensuring there is no attack surface. And this is the bit people miss: if there’s no shell and no interpreter, there’s nothing in the model weights that knows what to do next. That turns a drive-by (pick your framework’s RCE of the week and you’ve got a shell, and the model weights know what to do with shell access) into a targeted attack that needs your source code. you can just port the missing libraries now The classic objection: your unikernel needs to talk to Stripe, and OCaml doesn’t have a Stripe library. Before AI you’d sigh and write it. Now? Run a loop to port the Go library to OCaml. Here you go: Stripe in a unikernel. Justin had a great example of the same thing. He’d been building minimal Linux OS images for appliances, which is halfway to a unikernel anyway, since you’re only running one application as PID 1. He needed to make an XFS filesystem. Rather than drag in xfsprogs and everything it brings with it, he sat down with an agent and had it write mkfs.xfs in Rust, producing byte-for-byte identical output, with every flag interpreted. It reverse-engineered the on-disk formats one by one, with tests across block sizes. It took a few hours. That works because the original tool is a golden oracle. Generate filesystems at different sizes with both implementations and diff them. Port the tests across. Automate it. Storage was the other big gap. Most workloads these days are cloud-shaped, even on-prem, so take the turbopuffer approach: S3 as your primary, infinitely growable storage, with a local NVMe block cache and an LRU (or whatever caching algorithm you like) for the hot bits. Justin is a massive “S3 for everything” fan too. As long as latency isn’t the constraint, you get infinite storage with multi-user access, and you can build everything on it. nix machine tests and overlays Justin had been experimenting with Nix too, and was surprised that the first time he got an agent to prototype an OS, it built all the tests into flakes. Nix the language sucks. Nixpkgs is great. NixOS machine tests are the bee’s knees: you write a test that spins up a fleet of machines and exercises the interaction between your network rules and your application. It’s the thing people don’t know about. And when something upstream is broken, or there’s a supply chain problem in your dependencies, that’s just an overlay. If you have to tool-call a human, also known as “Dear Maintainer”, who might be on holiday or might have abandoned the project, and wait a day, two days, or even five minutes, that’s not AGI. We’re building recursive products here. Agents need the ability to modify the world as first-party source, not as third-party bundled binaries. We’re going back to the contrib folder and Unix patches. if you care about security, you have two choices Justin asked what unikernels still need for people to discover them. Honestly, it’s this. We’ve raised two generations of developers who don’t even know they’re a thing.

t: patch the planet
x: I don’t know if you’ve seen this, but a CA just got popped. Their keys got leaked, which means the industry as a whole now has some pretty major problems. It was revealed two hours ago. Now you’re probably wondering why I’m writing up this blog post. It’s simple. This is perhaps one of the easiest security patches I’ve ever done, and I’ve discovered a few new tricks. First, understand that fixing this with ease without Nix is almost impossible. Tens of millions of dollars (if not more) in productivity are being lost worldwide right now as everyone tries to patch their transitive dependencies. Meanwhile, because I’ve used Nix, I can patch the planet, since the ideas behind the blog post below extend into security as well. Because of Nix’s single source of truth and the ability to patch this single source of truth, I’m able to issue a simple prompt like this: okay is my nixos for my fleet affected by https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/? With results in the following. So the problem here is the transitive dependencies. It’s easy to patch one thing, but the transitive dependencies are the problem, and this is where Nix shines: one fix fixes the transitive dependencies automatically. One patch fixes the entire fleet and its transitive dependencies. Patch, commit, and autodeploy your fleet 🍻 the new trick Alright, I promised a new trick. Here’s the trick. You can prompt an agent to update the AGENTS.MD to automatically back out these patches, let’s say in five days from now, just by using the AGENTS.MD as a reminder 😎 So it was one simple prompt to identify if I was affected, which turned into a plan, which then automatically fixed it, and now, in a couple of days, it will reassess the situation, give time for the ecosystem and dust to settle, and then automatically back it out once all the upstream transitive dependencies have been resolved. Cool, huh? ## Temporary reminder: eMudhra root blacklist (from 2026-10-22) On or after 2026-10-22, check whether the `nixos-26.05` channel contains nixpkgs commit `7816d39` (the backported `security/ca.nix` distrust of the eMudhra roots), e.g. `nix eval --raw --refresh --impure --expr '(builtins.getFlake "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-26.05").rev'` then `git merge-base --is-ancestor`. If it does not, check again two days later. Once it does, back out the fleet-wide workaround: update the `nixpkgs` pin to include it, delete `nix/domains/system/public-trust.nix` (contract `fleet-distrust-emudhra-roots`) and its imports in `nix/domains/system/catalog.nix`, `nix/domains/artifacts/guest/configuration.nix` and the `host-kexec` modules in `flake.nix`, and remove the eMudhra paragraph from `marshall/priv/hldd/12-configuration.md`. Then verify that the built host and guest bundles still lack the four roots, and delete this section. Keep Marshall's system-store TLS defaults (`runtime-postgres-system-trust`, `mail-smtp-system-trust`) and the `rustls-webpki` update; they are not part of the workaround. I can’t stress this enough. If you build something, you own it, including all the dependencies you rely on. We’re entering weird times where cyber offensive models will be continuously on the attack. The game has changed. To defend, you need more inferencing capability than the attacker, and you also need to respond rapidly. This is by far the easiest security patch I’ve ever done, and the best part is I won’t carry this tech debt for long because an agent will automatically back it out in a couple of days.

t: Death to long-lived static credentials
x: Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you’d use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let’s Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic. OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers. At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers. Long-lived static credentials are insecure Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand. Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production. Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again. Better solutions already exist With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant. A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it. We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on. The rest of the web hasn’t followed We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods. But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption: Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key. Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path. Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication. Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it. Our commitment to a more secure web We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners. Make secure authentication easier to use Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it. With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports. import { getToken } from '@vercel/connect'; const token = await getToken('oauth/linear', { subject: { type: 'user', id: 'user_123' }, scopes: ['read'], }); Requesting Linear access for a user through Vercel Connect We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows. OIDC UI for API providers OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch. Generate trust-policy forms and token verification code for your service. Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical. Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls. For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key.
